title: UV robots, cotton bots & ChatGPT on a Broccoli farm: The new face of farming - YouTube

snippets.text: Right now in California, a fleet of
robots is hunting bugs on a strawberry
plant at 2:00 in the morning, zapping
pests with ultraviolet light instead of
pesticides. [music]
In China's Xinjiang Desert, cotton
fields larger than some countries are
partly being run by machines with barely
a human in sight.
>> [music]
>> In Nebraska, a 2-ft robot crawls across
the surface of a grain silo doing one of
the deadliest jobs in American farming
so human never has to.
And in northern Japan, a former
government worker with no coding
background and no family farm is running
a 100-hectare operation using ChatGPT.
The people who feed 8 billion of [music]
us are getting older. Farm labor is
getting scarcer, more expensive, and
climate stress is making every season
less predictable. And it's all happening
right now in 2026.
With massive investment in innovation
going into AI, robotics, and autonomy in
farming, this is looking ever more
likely to be the future of agriculture.
The question is, can they actually
transform how we grow food enough to
save this increasingly problematic
industry,
>> [music]
>> or are these just fun toys for the
oldest industry on Earth?
TRIC Robotics, out of San Luis Obispo in
California, builds autonomous robots
that patrol fields at night because
that's when ultraviolet C light kills
pests and mildew most effectively and
stresses the plant least.
The data claims the UVC and bug vacuum
combo cut lygus bugs by 35%, spotted
wing fruit flies by 58%, spider mites by
a third, and mildew pressure by 30% with
almost no spraying. [music]
Farmers don't even buy the
robots, they pay for it as a service.
Now, scale that up massively. In
Xinjiang, which grows around 90% of
China's cotton, the agritech company XAG
has been building super cotton fields.
Robots loaded with cameras, sensors, and
self-driving tech read each plant,
calculate the exact dose of fertilizer
or pesticides, and spray it precisely.
One robot covers nearly 7 hectares an
hour, and one technician can run five of
them at once.
By the end of 2025, this model has
spread across more than 130,000
hectares. And then there's the quieter
kind of robot, the one that saves lives.
Grain bins are actually one of the
deadliest parts of farming. Farmers get
trapped and suffocate in flowing grain
every single year.
So, a Nebraska father-and-son team built
the Grain Weevil,
a 2-ft robot that uses spinning augers
to create a controlled avalanche,
leveling and breaking up grain from the
outside, so no human ever climbs in.
They've already sold more than 100.
And the most surprising one, Hiroki
Tomiyasu in Hokkaido.
10 years ago, he was a public servant in
Tokyo.
No farm degree, no engineering degree.
Today, he manages 100 hectares of
broccoli, pumpkins, onions, and
soybeans, and he built his own software
to do it using ChatGPT and Codex. He
wired up a phone-controlled greenhouse
vent. He pulls satellite data to track
his own crop's health. He even
photographs black spots [music] on
broccoli heads and asks AI whether it's
a disease and what to do about it. Now,
none of this appeared overnight. The
road to the AI-integrated farm started
with something boring, GPS. In the
mid-1990s, John Deere, working with
NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, put
satellite receivers on tractors accurate
enough to drive them in near-perfect
straight lines. That gave farmers yield
maps showing exactly which parts of the
field produced more and which parts
produced less.
Once you can measure every single square
meter, you can treat every square meter
differently. That is the whole idea
behind precision agriculture. Variable
rates of seed, water, and fertilizer
instead of blanketing the whole field
the same way. The leap to AI came in
2017 when Deere paid 305 million for a
startup [music]
called Blue River Technology. It's
seeing spray system uses cameras and
[music] computer vision to tell a crop
from a weed, scanning over a million
plants an hour, and sprays only the
weeds. In 2022, John Deere unveiled a
fully autonomous tractor at CES. 16
cameras giving 360°
vision, GPS accurate to less than an
inch, no driver in the cab at all.
So, where does AI actually help?
Broadly, in four places.
First, seeing. Computer vision now spots
pests and disease early, often with 90%
accuracy, so a farmer can treat one sick
patch instead of the whole field.
Second, predicting.
Machine learning models forecast yields,
disease rates, soil nutrients, and
perfect time to irrigate, turning
weather and series data into decisions.
Third, acting on the information they
gather.
Robots and smart sprayers do the
physical work.
Selective weeding can cut herbicide use
by up to 95%.
Farms using these tools report up to 20%
higher yields and around 20% lower input
costs. [music] And fourth, advising.
This is the newest one. Generative AI,
like the tool that broccoli farmer uses,
turns the chatbot into an on-call
agronomist, translator, and software
engineer rolled into one. But, how does
the robot actually tell a weed from a
lettuce? It starts with cameras, usually
regular color cameras, plus near
infrared and sometimes hyperspectral
sensors that see wavelengths our eyes
can't.
Healthy plants, stressed plants, and
bare soil all reflect light differently.
Those images feed a deep learning model,
often a convolutional neural network or
a YOLO detector, trained on hundreds of
thousands of labeled plant images.
In milliseconds, it segments the frames,
draws a box around each plant, and
classifies it, crop or weed. Then comes
the action. The software fires an
actuator, a precisely aimed nozzle spot
sprays the weed, or a mechanical tool
rips it out, all while the machine is
still moving.
Every robot is a variation on this loop,
sense, decide, act. The Green Weevil
swaps cameras for an auger and a
controlled avalanche of physics. TRIC
swaps sprayers for UVC light and a
vacuum. John Deere's driverless tractor
wraps the whole thing in an
inch-accurate GPS and 360° vision. Same
recipe, different tools. So, if the tech
works this well, why isn't every farm
automated?
Because there's a catch, several
actually. First, cost. Autonomous robots
and the hardware around them are wildly
expensive, [music]
often out of reach for anyone but the
largest commercial operations.
It's exactly why companies like [music]
TRIC rent the robots as a service
instead of selling it. Most farmers
simply can't buy one outright.
Second, connectivity. A huge share of
these robots need reliable broadband and
cloud [music] access, which vast
stretches of rural farmland simply do
not have.
This is the digital divide drawn across
the countryside. Third, skills. Somebody
has to operate, maintain, and trust
[music] these systems, and rural
training and digital literacy haven't
kept pace.
And fourth, fit. Most of this tech was
designed big uniform single crop fields.
It doesn't map neatly into the small
mixed crop plots that feed much of the
world. Plus, there's real worries about
who owns that farm data.
So, can AI and robotics really transform
agriculture? The answer is yes, but
unevenly.
The money says the shift is real. The AI
in agriculture market [music] was worth
roughly $2.5 billion in 2025 and is
projected to grow towards 25 [music]
billion within a decade.
This isn't a passing fad. The capability
is here and it works.
But the constraint was never the
engineering. It's access and economics.
The industrial cotton fields of Xinjiang
and the big farms [music] of the
American Midwest will automate first
because they have the scale to justify
the costs. The real wild card is that
broccoli farmer in Hokkaido [music]
because generative AI is quietly
dropping the barrier, letting one
curious [music] person do what used to
need a whole engineering team. If that
keeps up, the next farm revolution might
not come from a $500,000 robot, but from
a chatbot in a farmer's pocket. The
technology to transform farming already
exists. However, over the next decade,
we'll see who gets to use it and how it
will impact our food.
